video_title: Eclipse's Lior Susan on $12.5B AUM and the Bet on Physical Industries
gist: Eclipse Ventures founder Lior Susan explains the firm's 'operators with capital' model for investing in and incubating physical-industry companies (chips, energy, robotics, defense), arguing that 85% of world GDP sits in the physical economy while venture capital has been starved of it, and that Eclipse's vertically-integrated 'Eclipse economy' portfolio lets it compete with China's state-aligned industrial buildout.

insights.claim: 85% of world GDP, roughly $100 trillion, sits in the physical world, which Eclipse Ventures uses as the core justification for concentrating capital in physical industries rather than software.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Frames a structural capital-allocation gap: investors overweight the ~15% of GDP that is software/services and underweight the 85% that is physical, implying a long runway for hard-tech venture returns.
insights.quote: What you cannot fight against is 85% of the world GDP, roughly 100 trillion, is in the physical world.

insights.claim: Metal manufacturing alone is a roughly $3 trillion industry, yet Lior Susan estimates total software/venture capital combined focused on it is under $20 billion, illustrating a massive capital misallocation versus market size.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A multi-trillion-dollar industry with sub-$20B of capital attention is a textbook underinvested category for a hard-tech fund to mine for outsized returns.

insights.claim: China built an estimated $20 trillion economy on physical industries by deliberately aligning five forces — talent, policy, capital, technology, and customer demand — into a self-reinforcing economic flywheel, which Lior Susan says is very difficult for a standalone Western company to compete against alone.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Explains why Eclipse pursues an integrated, multi-company ecosystem strategy (the 'Eclipse economy') rather than backing isolated point solutions — it's trying to replicate China's flywheel inside a Western venture portfolio.

insights.claim: Lior Susan's original 2015 thesis was that deglobalization would force countries to stop relying on other nations for energy, manufacturing, and defense, but he admits he was wrong about timing — it took much longer than expected, with COVID acting as the real catalyst that exposed supply-chain vulnerability and kicked off reshoring.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A rare admission that a founding thesis was directionally right but years early — useful calibration for investors judging how long reindustrialization theses take to pay off.
insights.quote: It was clear to me that it's going to happen. Now I was wrong on the time took much longer than I thought. Kind of COVID was the really first one that showed the vulnerability.

insights.claim: Lior Susan believes the US could grow GDP 5-7% annually if capital, talent, government support, customer demand, and technology are fully mobilized behind building physical industries, and describes the current period as the best time in the country's history to build companies since Henry Ford and Carnegie.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Sets an explicit, checkable macro growth target tied to industrial-policy and hard-tech buildout that investors can track against actual GDP prints.
insights.quote: I do believe us can grow five six 7% every year... this is the best time in the history of this country to build companies.

insights.claim: Lior Susan argues that building physical infrastructure like data centers creates a broad local economic flywheel (construction, energy, housing, restaurants, service providers), and calls local pushback against new data centers self-defeating.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A pro-development framing investors can use to gauge political/regulatory risk to data center and industrial buildouts — he expects (and wants) opposition to fade as job-creation benefits are recognized.
insights.quote: When you build a data center in Nebraska, you create thousands of jobs and it's a circular economy... the whole flywheel of their economy is actually kicking in.

themes.theme: Eclipse's operating model and incubation engine

insights.claim: Eclipse Ventures describes itself as 'operators with capital' rather than a traditional VC, staffed by former industry operators who sit hands-on with portfolio companies on manufacturing, supply chain, capex, government relations, subsidies, and debt-versus-equity decisions rather than providing passive capital.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Signals Eclipse's differentiated value-add versus generalist or 'tourist' VCs newly entering hard tech — relevant for founders picking investors and for LPs assessing durability of Eclipse's edge.
insights.quote: We never thought maybe ourselves as a venture capital. We call it operators with capital because we are operators with capital.

insights.claim: Of Eclipse's roughly 90 total portfolio companies, about 30 were directly built/incubated by Eclipse itself rather than sourced as external deals, via a deliberate in-house venture-equity/incubation strategy.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A one-third incubation rate is unusually high for a VC firm; investors evaluating Eclipse funds should weight incubated-company risk/reward differently than passive co-investments.

insights.claim: Lior Susan says Eclipse deliberately avoids formal portfolio construction (e.g., mandating one defense company, one chip company, one robotics company) and instead invests only in companies the team is personally obsessed with, rejecting inbound requests to fill thematic slots.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Pushes back against the standard LP diligence question about diversification/portfolio construction — useful context for LPs assessing concentration risk in Eclipse funds versus other multi-stage funds.
insights.quote: My portfolio construction is not to have a portfolio construction... I actually don't must have anything. I must have the companies I'm obsessed with.

insights.claim: Eclipse's robotics company Mind was spun out of Rivian after roughly three years of informal conversations between Lior Susan and Rivian's RJ (a robotics team lead), formalized at a robotics dinner at Susan's house; spinning out let the company raise external capital off Rivian's balance sheet and attract engineering talent that wouldn't otherwise join Rivian, while positioning it as a neutral 'Switzerland' vendor able to work with multiple manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A repeatable playbook — spin out internal corporate robotics/hard-tech teams into independently capitalized, vendor-neutral startups — that investors should watch for at other large industrial/OEM companies.
insights.quote: You can win all wars. We can attract better talent that will not necessarily go work today for that problem inside Rivian; we can attract external capital so it's not on your balance sheet, and it's like a Switzerland.

insights.claim: Eclipse's founders (Lior Susan and Pierre Lamond) personally do hands-on operational firefighting for portfolio companies, such as Susan flying to a Midwest data center for 72 hours to personally coordinate fixes for a major water-cooling leak, including installing new HVAC systems and managing concrete-drying to prevent moisture damage to electronics.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Illustrates the literal, operational depth of Eclipse's 'operators with capital' claim — a form of investor value-add that is difficult for capital-only competitors to replicate at scale.
insights.quote: I was there 72 hours without my family, anything else, just on the floor till that thing got fixed.

themes.theme: Valuation framework: physical industries vs. SaaS

insights.claim: Lior Susan argues that free cash flow, not gross margin, is what actually drives public-market valuation (EPS/trading multiples), and that gross margin is only an indicator of potential future free cash flow.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Investors benchmarking hard-tech companies against SaaS gross-margin norms are using the wrong yardstick; free cash flow generation potential should be the comparison point instead.
insights.quote: What matters is free cash flow. It's actually not gross margin. Gross margin is an indicator to potentially what your free cash flow going to be.

insights.claim: Lior Susan claims many SaaS companies' apparent high gross margins are partly an accounting artifact from reclassifying engineering spend from COGS into R&D, whereas physical-industry companies face a 'hard cog' that accountants won't let them hide, meaning reported margins understate true operating discipline.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to using headline SaaS gross margins as a quality signal; investors comparing hard-tech and software unit economics should adjust for this accounting difference.
insights.quote: We mechanically move the engineering spend from what's supposed to be in a cogs... to an R&D and it was an accounting trick. So your gross margin is high but you still needs to continue hire engineers.

insights.claim: Lior Susan's investment screen for any company, physical or otherwise, is: is the addressable market meaningfully above $20 billion, is the company sufficiently differentiated within it, and does the team have the ability to solve a genuinely hard problem — citing Tesla (mid-teens gross margin, trades like top SaaS names) and Cerebras (40-50% gross margin, trades better than most SaaS companies) as proof that market size and differentiation, not gross margin, drive premium valuation.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, three-factor underwriting checklist (>$20B TAM, differentiation, team capability) investors can apply to screen hard-tech deals regardless of margin profile.
insights.quote: I always ask the trick question: how big is the market— 20 billion is not big enough— how differentiated is what you do in that market, and do you have the right team to actually go and solve that really tough problem.

insights.claim: Lior Susan notes that despite thousands of SaaS/CRM companies competing in a roughly $30 billion CRM market, the memory chip industry has only three major players (Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung) despite a market experiencing a severe shortage, because the capital intensity, engineering depth, and structural barriers ('five forces') make memory far harder to enter than software.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Highlights an oligopoly with real pricing power and a persistent shortage — exactly the kind of structurally protected, underserved market Eclipse says it is targeting with new memory-company investments.
insights.quote: There's like 10,000 SaaS companies... how it can be that there's only three memory companies... we are building a new memory companies.

themes.theme: The 'Eclipse economy': vertically integrated portfolio leverage

insights.claim: Eclipse deliberately builds a vertically integrated 'Eclipse economy' spanning chips, AI servers, racks/CPUs (Oxide), data centers, energy sources (nuclear, sodium-ion, lithium-ion, gas turbines), and applied/physical AI for robotics and manufacturing, so that portfolio companies can jointly serve the same large customer deals.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A distinctive structural moat: an investor evaluating any single Eclipse portfolio company should check whether it benefits from bundled demand across sibling portfolio companies, which can accelerate growth beyond what a standalone cap table would suggest.

insights.claim: Because Eclipse can route large commercial deals across three or four portfolio companies simultaneously, Lior Susan says a single dollar of committed capital effectively becomes four to five dollars of value captured across the 'Eclipse economy,' and this cross-portfolio involvement also gives Eclipse influence over how large deals and related policy get structured.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Investors should treat Eclipse's deal-flow advantage (privileged access plus deal-shaping influence) as a structural edge over competing funds bidding for the same physical-industry deals.
insights.quote: You have a $1 that became four five dollars because naturally you are leveraging multiple of your companies... we can shape how those very large deals is happening or how this policy is happening.

insights.claim: Eclipse's portfolio signed roughly $40-50 billion in commercial deals across the portfolio in the past year, with some individual deals reaching double-digit billions in total contract value.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A concrete scale metric for underwriting Eclipse's portfolio revenue pipeline and cross-selling leverage, useful for LPs sizing expected fund performance.

insights.claim: Lior Susan lays out a recurring 'second act / third act' pattern in successful physical-industry companies: Cerebras moved from chips to systems to running data centers; SpaceX moved from launch to Starlink; Redwood Materials moved from battery recycling to selling large-scale energy storage; True Anomaly moved from space-domain awareness to vertically integrated defense programs like Golden Dome.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A repeatable expansion pattern investors can use to forecast follow-on revenue lines and valuation step-ups in physical-industry portfolio companies rather than viewing their first product as the ceiling.
insights.quote: When you build something in the physical world, you actually if you are successful, you will have the ability to introduce multiple of new businesses that will grow your wallet share in that sector.

insights.claim: Eclipse identified that gas turbine lead times have stretched to roughly five years with the whole industry fully backlogged, and used that bottleneck — discovered through its own data-center buildouts — as the basis to launch a new large gas-turbine company to compete directly with incumbents like GE Vernova.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: A concrete, sourceable supply bottleneck (5-year turbine lead times) that is currently constraining data-center/power buildouts and creating room for new entrants — worth monitoring for both the incumbent's pricing power and the new entrant's ramp.
insights.quote: We saw that gas turbine lead time is insane. Five years, fully backlogged the whole companies, and we're like oh we actually deploying a lot of them, we should go build a modern company to do gas turbine.

themes.theme: Portfolio company specifics: Redwood Materials and Oxide

insights.claim: Redwood Materials pivoted from battery recycling toward selling large-scale battery-based energy storage to data centers, a move Eclipse says was well timed to when Chinese firms (including CATL) began facing restrictions on selling energy storage into the US grid; Redwood recently hired Deepak Ahuja, Tesla's former longtime CFO, reinforcing its Tesla-alumni leadership team alongside CEO JB Straubel.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Flags a policy-driven market opening (restrictions on Chinese energy-storage suppliers) that domestic players like Redwood Materials can capture, and signals management-quality upgrade via the ex-Tesla CFO hire.

insights.claim: Oxide Computer builds on-premises, CPU-based server racks with a cloud-like software experience, based on Eclipse's thesis that not all workloads will move to the public cloud due to security, latency, and cost concerns; Lior Susan says Eclipse did not foresee the AI boom when investing but the AI-driven on-prem/sovereign-compute demand has accelerated Oxide's growth, with customers ranging from double-digit millions of dollars up to one customer at 'many hundreds or billions' in contract value.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Validates on-prem/sovereign AI infrastructure as a durable, non-consensus bet that got a tailwind from an unrelated trend (AI), and gives a revenue-concentration data point (one whale account driving outsized contract value) worth tracking for customer-concentration risk.
insights.quote: We didn't know that AI will be a thing to be clear. So getting lucky is important in this business.

insights.claim: Eclipse co-founder Pierre Lamond, an 85-year-old former 35-year Sequoia Capital partner (with earlier roots at Fairchild and National Semiconductor alongside Don Valentine), joined Lior Susan in 2015 within about four months of their first meeting to found Eclipse, worked full-time in the office for seven years, and instilled a culture of extreme operational discipline drawn from his semiconductor and venture background.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Explains the institutional-grade governance and board discipline Eclipse applies from day one (rare for an 11-year-old fund) as a direct inheritance from old-guard Sequoia practices, relevant to LPs assessing firm maturity.
insights.quote: Discipline, discipline, discipline... you cannot fake it till you make it when you're manufacturing something because the yield will just be very bad.

insights.claim: Lior Susan says he has spent significant time with OpenAI's Sam Altman over the past year and considers him a major source of personal and professional inspiration, viewing OpenAI's and Anthropic's work as foundational to Eclipse's own ability to build more physical-AI companies.
insights.speaker: Lior Susan
insights.so_what: Signals a close informal relationship between a leading physical-industry investor and OpenAI's leadership, suggesting alignment/collaboration potential between frontier AI labs and Eclipse's physical-AI portfolio companies.
insights.quote: A lot of the things that OpenAI did and others and Anthropic and other amazing companies are really important to our ability to build more companies.
